confidence_note: Theory and experiment verified in the archive.org full text (chapter 'Dreaming as Overnight Therapy'). The REM/noradrenaline mechanism is Walker's theory with supporting evidence, not settled fact. Walker presents prazosin as approved for trauma nightmares, but a large 2018 VA trial (Raskind et al., NEJM) found it no better than placebo; the story states this caveat. Old PTSD/anxiety/depression causal chain and the 'sleep is therapeutic' quote dropped.
facts: Walker set out to test the saying that time heals all wounds, suspecting it was time spent in dream sleep.

During REM sleep the stress chemical noradrenaline is completely shut off in the brain, the only time in twenty-four hours, while emotion and memory regions like the amygdala and hippocampus reactivate.
Experiment: healthy young adults viewed emotional images in an MRI scanner twice, twelve hours apart; half viewed morning then evening while awake, half evening then the next morning after sleep.
Those who slept reported significantly less emotion and showed a large drop in amygdala reactivity, with the prefrontal cortex re-engaged; the awake group's reactions were as strong or stronger.
The quality of REM sleep, reflecting the drop in stress chemistry, predicted who got the overnight relief.
Walker's phrase: REM sleep is 'sleeping to remember' the details and 'sleeping to forget' the painful emotional charge.
Dr. Murray Raskind at a VA hospital near Seattle gave veterans with PTSD the blood-pressure drug prazosin and their recurring nightmares eased; prazosin suppresses noradrenaline in the brain.
A large 2018 trial in veterans with chronic PTSD found prazosin no better than placebo for nightmares.

Walker's illustration: most of our strongest childhood memories are emotional (being separated from parents, nearly being hit by a car), yet recalling them no longer brings back the same intensity; he credits REM sleep for stripping the emotion while keeping the memory.
Raskind's patients returned after a few weeks of treatment saying, in effect, 'Doc, it's the strangest thing, my dreams don't have those flashback nightmares anymore.'
Walker argues that if REM sleep did not do this, every recall of a salient memory would bring back the same stressful charge, leaving us in chronic anxiety.
scene_details: the MRI scanner and the same emotional images twelve hours later
tension: Same images, same twelve hours; only one group got upset all over again.
opening_idea: Open with the saying 'time heals all wounds' and Walker deciding to test it in a scanner.

lessons.idea: Give a painful day a night of sleep before deciding how you feel about it.
lessons.anchor: The awake group stayed as reactive; the sleep group calmed.
lessons.example: After a harsh comment from a boss, someone writes the reply but waits until after a night's sleep to send it.

reflect_final: What recent upsetting moment did you judge late at night, and how did it look the next morning?

use_cases.situation: A friend wants to settle an argument at midnight.
use_cases.move: Mention Walker's scanner study: after a night's sleep the same images hit less hard; suggest talking tomorrow.

use_cases.situation: A family row is escalating in the evening.
use_cases.move: Propose pausing until breakfast and say why.

use_cases.situation: You are replaying a bad moment in bed.
use_cases.move: Note the decision you're tempted to make and look at it again in the morning.

pocket_idea: The same upsetting images hit less after a night's sleep; let REM work before you reply.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In REM sleep the brain's stress chemical noradrenaline shuts off completely, the only time it does all day.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Walker scanned people looking at upsetting images twice, twelve hours apart; those who slept in between reacted far less, those awake did not. REM sleep, with noradrenaline off, seems to strip the emotional charge.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Has a problem ever looked smaller the next morning?
